utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please address the matter that you intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the -- I said, and that remains the position, that there wasn't anything specific to the witness currently giving evidence which caused any difficulty about open session. The -- the matter of Mr. Krajisnik's request to ask questions himself by way of cross-examination has, of course, arisen in the first place specifically in relation to this witness, but it is more general. Your Honour -- Your Honour is quite right in the reference made just a moment ago while the blinds or curtains were coming up to refer to the fact that of course it gives rise to the whole question of relations between counsel and the accused. Your Honour, the -- there is one highly exceptional case at the moment in front of this Tribunal, Mr. Milosevic's case, but I must admit I haven't got time to follow Milosevic's case as well in enormous detail but it's impossible not to be aware of developments in that case. That's a wholly exceptional situation, as Your Honour is aware. There it's quite clear Mr. Milosevic does not want counsel. Counsel have been imposed upon him, so it's an utterly different situation, and Mr. Milosevic is not giving instructions to those counsel. So it's totally different. Mr. Krajisnik has requested counsel in this case, has requested assignment of counsel, and I as lead counsel and then Ms. Loukas as co-counsel have been assigned. The code of conduct that we are under, and this actually applies to our own domestic codes from our own bars as well as the code of conduct applicable for this Tribunal reflects the clear understanding that we as counsel have the conduct of the case. Now, Your Honour will know from Your Honour's own experience that of course there is a -- there is a borderline, there is a margin at which there can be legitimate debate about whether something falls on the line of client -- on one side of the line, the client's instructions, or the conduct of the case, but that particular border area is not, in fact, the practical difficulty between counsel and client. In this sort of case, the practical area of discussion, to put it gently and mildly between counsel and client, is actually to do with the client understanding what that actually means in practice and understanding that counsel, having the conduct of the case, actually does mean that, and it means that counsel do get to decide how the case is presented, how to go about it. The -- Your Honour referred to having survived 17 years in a system which would be unfamiliar to me. I confess that. Your Honour, we do aim -- we -- at the moment we are, in a sense, struggling to survive in many respects in this case. We would strongly urge that we are given something other than mere survival in the handling of this very difficult case. It's not necessary, not appropriate for me to enter into any confidential discussions between Mr. Krajisnik and me. That would be quite wrong as to actual content or substance of the case, but what I do feel able to say is that, perhaps not surprising, given that Mr. Krajisnik is on any footing a -- we can see that from the evidence, he's a strong character and intelligent man. It's not surprising that some fairly tough talking would have taken place over a pretty long period between Mr. Krajisnik and me when I first came into the case, particularly in the circumstances, the slightly unhappy circumstances in which Mr. Krajisnik had to have a change of counsel team. The demarcation and the understanding and the explanation and, in the end, bluntly an assertion that that was the way it was under the code of conduct and that is the way which cases have to be conducted, that involved some very long, tough talking. Mr. Krajisnik, I said yesterday and I stand by this, of course we have our moments within the Defence team, no doubt it even happens within the Prosecution team, of course there are strong disagreements from time to time and they get resolved. Naturally there are strong disagreements between Mr. Krajisnik and me, but the general working relations are pretty good. But it is not going to help the conduct of this case one bit for anybody, and certainly not for Mr. Krajisnik, if we now depart, after that protracted discussion, if we now depart from the clear understanding that if Mr. Krajisnik wishes a point to be presented in his defence before this Tribunal, he needs to instruct his counsel clearly as to that point, and then it is our job to form our professional assessment about how best to present that case both on that point, both on the strategic level, because this is a marathon, not a sprint, and on the tactical day-to-day level. And that exercise is severely undermined if we are not able to be confident that Mr. Krajisnik at least understands - whether he likes it or not is another matter - Mr. Krajisnik at least understands that that is the way it should be done. Because if we are, after all this time, now thrown back to a position where Mr. Krajisnik feels -- I'm not suggesting Mr. Krajisnik is going to do anything deliberately underhand or anything like that - I'm not suggesting that for one moment - but if Mr. Krajisnik feels, well, all right, I don't -- I don't actually need to tell my counsel this, I don't need to tell them everything, I don't need to be frank with them because I have the opportunity now of stepping in and I have the opportunity of asking questions. I, Mr. Krajisnik, have that reserve option, if you like. That is going to be immensely damaging to the conduct of this case on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik, and it is going to be contrary to his interests. It's absolutely plain that we don't like it, Your Honour. From our own professional, personal position, we would hate this. That's -- that's not the acid test, although we wouldn't like it perhaps to be totally disregarded because it's not the Trial Chamber's job to make our life easy, but we do request the Trial Chamber does what it can to make our life no more difficult than it already is in this area. But the fundamental point is it is just not the right, effective, proper way in Mr. Krajisnik's interests and then indirectly in the interests of justice and the interests of the Tribunal and the Trial Chamber to do it this way. The -- it's also, we comment, it would -- as Your Honour indicates, it would be unprecedented if we leave aside that very special situation - and the particular solution there is perhaps not exactly what's being talked about here - that very special situation in Mr. Milosevic's case. Is this going to become a general practice? Otherwise, what is the reason for Mr. Krajisnik, apart from the fact that this is what he would want to do, what is the reason for Mr. Krajisnik being given this special dispensation? It arose in the context of his concern about inadequate preparation in relation to a witness. But as a matter of fact, a client is nearly always going to feel that that is so, because inevitably in a complicated case there will be, because we're only human, there will always be areas that the client feels that his counsel has not absorbed, has not understood, has not covered. There's a post-mortem in relation to many cross-examinations. Sometimes the post-mortem, if post-mortems can have a happy result, sometimes the post-mortem has the happy result that all those questions that the client was insistent should be asked he now sees didn't need to be asked or were even better not asked. Sometimes the post-mortem has the result that the client still feels dissatisfied. Maybe sometimes the client might be right about that. Quite often the client isn't right about it. Your Honour is very familiar with these extremely difficult judgements. But if these judgements are split in this way, the result is complete chaos, and we do urge upon the Tribunal that this is a retrograde step to allow it. It may appear spuriously to be an attractive freedom and an attractive opportunity to give to a defendant, but on analysis it is absolutely and fundamentally the wrong way of dealing with the matter. Mr. Krajisnik has counsel. As a matter of fact, he's applied to remove us as counsel, and we are taking a neutral position on that as things stand absolutely at this moment because we are committed to Mr. Krajisnik's defence, we are committed to doing it in a professional way, having the conduct of the case on the basis of his instructions, and we have indicated to the Registry that we will abide by the Registry's decision on that. So we neither support nor oppose Mr. Krajisnik's application, but we think it's fair, without getting into that, we think it's fair to say that Mr. Krajisnik's application is not fundamentally based on a suggestion that we are not competent. It seems not to be that at all. And certainly if there were any suggestion that that were part of the basis of Mr. Krajisnik's application, either to this Tribunal now on this particular point or more generally, that would be a much bigger issue. But we don't understand that to be an element of anything. And in those circumstances if we take the assumption in our own favour, if we make the assumption that we are at least professionally competent, the case should simply proceed in the normal way. Mr. Krajisnik has his right under the Statute, he has his fundamental right to be represented and present his case through counsel as the alternative that he has chosen, the alternative to his initial right; he could have done the case himself, but he has asked for assignment of counsel, and at the moment he has counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. First of all, I notice that Mr. Krajisnik would like to perhaps add something to what just has been said, but before giving an opportunity to do so, Mr. Hannis, I'd like to know whether the Prosecution would take any specific position in what seems to be not directly a problem which affects the Prosecution, although questioning, of course, could have some impact on the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought about what our response would be if we were asked. It is -- it's difficult because I'm not sure what our standing is to take a position in regard to this matter. I do know from my brief tenure as a public defender many years ago I had a situation like this where it occurred and the Judge permitted the defendant to play an active role and it was very -- as a practical matter, very difficult to try and manage that because the client is taking one tack and the lawyer is taking another and it can create some severe problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this sounds more as an expression of sympathy with Mr. Stewart than -- but I'd like to know the position whether the Prosecution at all takes a position, because of course these are Prosecution witnesses. If cross-examined by or at least put questions in cross-examination by Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to know whether there's any clear position apart from understanding of what it means for counsel, whether the Prosecution takes a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what I would like to do now is take no position but reserve the opportunity to perhaps respond later if this matter gets a continuing discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So for the time being no position by the Prosecution. I think, looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just consulted with the other Judges whether we should grant the request of Mr. Krajisnik to express himself, at least to either respond or add something. We will briefly allow Mr. Krajisnik to make some observations. Mr. Krajisnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to address you. I agree with Mr. Stewart in the greatest part of what he just said, although he exaggerates our differences a little. Mr. Stewart doesn't believe in me, but I believe in him. That's the difference. However, the point is this: I would be happy if my counsel were prepared to examine this witness. Why would I ask to add some questioning myself? I would satisfy myself with just directing certain questions to my counsel. However, there is a number of witnesses who are crucial for getting at the truth. It is for the sake of getting at the truth that it is essential for this witness to be examined properly. It is a technical problem that I'm completely excluded from the process of my counsel's preparation because of the language barrier, among other things. Yesterday, we spent together 90 minutes. We did not manage to settle one single issue because Mr. Stewart does not understand the peculiarities dealt with by this witness. Whatever you decide, I know that you are well-intentioned. But I just had a laugh a second ago. The Prosecutor would be happy if what my counsel -- if what my counsel was saying were true, that I would hurt myself. This witness would be telling the truth, and you will decide as you wish, but I beg you to allow this at least as an experiment. If you decide otherwise, I know that you are well-intentioned anyway, and thank Mr. Hannis -- I thank Mr. Hannis here, because I appreciate his approach, his approach being that what matters is to get at the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. We will adjourn until ten minutes past eleven, and a decision will follow before the start of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I was informed that you would like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. I asked that we resume in open session because during the break I raised this issue with my fellow senior trial attorneys on this case and some of the supervisors in the case because we saw that the Court's decision regarding this matter could have implications beyond this case, for other cases as well as the institution. So I was asked to come back and advise the Court that the matter is being discussed in my office and we would like to have the opportunity to address certain issues to the Court before you decide. I understood that the Court intended to decide before we begin cross-examination, but I didn't know if you were going to decide immediately when we came back in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but when could you, because I think it would be fair that both the accused -- the accused and Defence counsel would know at the beginning of the cross-examination what -- what position the Chamber takes. So therefore, when could you make your submissions? Right away or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do you need some more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we will need some more time, and I anticipated I was going to finish my cross -- I mean my direct examination before the end of the day, even possibly before the end of this next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In which case we would need to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll give you an opportunity to -- to make further oral submissions and therefore will have a short break after the -- after the examination-in-chief has -- is concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have to return into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you announced that you would give the position of the Prosecution, and since we are in open session at this moment, it's the position of the Prosecution on whether or not to grant the request of the accused to put questions during cross-examination to the witness we are hearing at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your last remark, Your Honour, indicates to me only as to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would like to put it in a more broader context, of course. If a decision will be taken in respect of this witness it might cast some shadows. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We first of all start by recognising the Trial Chamber's, the Court's innate authority to determine how the trial should proceed in the course of the presentation of evidence. That's entirely within the Court's discretion. The proposed change that is being asked for here by Mr. Krajisnik is a significant change, we urge, that would be a big change in Tribunal jurisprudence. I understand Milosevic is a special case, at least we always speak of it as being a special case in that regard. And this is happening sort of not midstream in this case, fairly far along in this case. On the other hand, we understand that exceptional circumstances can justify a change. We would argue, however, Your Honour, that by allowing the proposed change, we have a concern that in essence it's giving the Defence two bites of the apple if his counsel is able to ask questions of a witness and then, when he's finished, Mr. Krajisnik is able to ask questions. We know it's a concern of all of us being able to move through this proceeding as efficiently and quickly as possible, so time constraints are a factor. We think that some of Mr. Krajisnik's concerns really can be satisfied if he's given an opportunity to consult with his counsel on these particular witnesses. I understand he has a concern about the ability of his lawyers to be as knowledgeable about a particular witness like the pending witness given the amount of time they've had to spend on this case. This is something that the defendant knows by heart because he's lived it. He's known these people for years, he knows it better than anyone else possibly could. And no one could expect his counsel to know it that well, but we think that if Mr. Krajisnik has additional questions that he would like to be presented to the witness, it can be done through his counsel. In the end, Your Honour, I think the Court has to strike a balance between the orderly and efficient conduct of trial, between the defendant's right to a fair trial, and also the rights and concerns of victims and witnesses who come to testify, because that can have an impact on them as well. If Your Honours do decide to allow the procedure in this case, we would -- we would request or urge the Court consider doing it with very tight controls, perhaps trying it only with one witness to see how it goes. We suggest it would not be appropriate or necessary or efficient to allow it with all witnesses. For example, a crime base witness from a small village in the hills of Bosnia would not be a witness that Mr. Krajisnik would personally have to cross-examine. It makes more sense with a witness like the present one. In addition, we have questions about if you do adopt it, Your Honours, how do we deal with what we've been calling the 60 per cent rule in our case where you allow Defence approximately 60 per cent of the time spent on direct examination for cross-examination. Does Mr. Krajisnik get 60 per cent and Mr. Stewart get 60 per cent? Do they divide the 60 per cent 50/50? How do we do that? In addition, it may have an impact on scheduling and planning of witnesses. Your Honour I hope realises that we have tried our very best to be efficient in estimating times for how long witnesses will take and not having witnesses sit around here and then having to go home and come back the next week. With an additional cross-examiner and one who is not a lawyer and for whom we don't yet have a feel of how his cross-examination would go and whether he would the full 60 per cent or none, it could have a bearing on such mundane matters as scheduling and planning. And finally, the last thing, Your Honour, I would ask if you do decide to allow it with regard to this particular witness, I would ask that before we resume with him or before the cross-examination begins, that the Court advise a witness that Mr. Krajisnik is going to cross-examine him, because during the course of our proofing, out of curiosity the witness asked me about the procedures before Court, and I told him I would ask him questions, the Defence counsel would ask him questions, then the Court would ask him questions, and he would be done and he would not be asked questions by Mr. Krajisnik. So this would come as a surprise to him, and I would ask the Court advise him of that before it happens so he doesn't think that I've misled him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, since there's fairly substantial contribution by the Prosecution, I would ask for the opportunity of dealing with a couple points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, we're a little bit taken aback, as it appeared Mr. Hannis was, by the suggestion that there might be a just ruling in relation to this particular witness. Really it follows from many of the submissions this morning that we really do, with respect, need and want to have a very clear position on this. The absolutely disastrous position is going to be if we an ad hoc position in relation to every witness where we will presumably then have -- if in principle -- we're inviting Your Honours in principle to reject this whole suggestion as simply unworkable and unhelpful, but if you should be tempted down the other course, we will just have perpetual conflict and dispute and debate and complete mess if every time Mr. Krajisnik feels there is a witness that he should have a go at as well we have this particular debate. Actually, the question -- I rather agree, with respect, with Mr. Hannis that as far as the crime base witnesses are concerned one wouldn't suppose that there would be any particular interest for Mr. Krajisnik, but in a way that illustrates the drawbacks of this procedure, because presumably it is going to be what Mr. Krajisnik sees as the more important witnesses in which he's going to want to exercise this right. So far as this particular witness is concerned, we also don't see -- or submit that it's not clear what's exceptional about this witness. He is -- he is in the category, obviously, of the more substantial witnesses rather than a large number of crime base witnesses, but this particular complaint, in effect, that Mr. Krajisnik is making is actually a familiar complaint. It's just that on this particular occasion it's been conversed into a request which in a sense is lurking there all the time in Mr. Krajisnik's attitude toward witnesses. He is, as I've indicated as many clients do - I don't blame him for this, Your Honour - he's always complaining that we haven't covered the ground, that we don't know enough. That's what clients do in complicated cases. But the -- we -- we -- excuse me one moment. Yes. The last observation I wanted to make was this, Your Honour, in relation to Mr. Hannis's questions about -- perfectly reasonable questions about what happens about the 60 per cent guideline. I don't suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can already answer that. Whatever the decision will be, there certainly will be no more time for cross-examination as is given now to the Defence. So whatever our decision will be, it's not even considered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that and would endorse it and was really going to make a submission along those lines on the basis that they are -- it is a guideline, of course, in every case, but in fact what it leads on to is this point, which is also, if you like, a corollary of what we were saying this morning, that what happens to our conduct of the case as counsel? Because when it comes to cross-examination normally, I decide -- I hope in proper consultation, but I decide whether co-counsel's going to cross-examine this witness, whether I'm going to cross-examine this witness. That's what I do. What do I do about this? Do I negotiate every time with my own client what the split's going to be? And imagine the work involved in sitting down together then instead of actually usefully working on the instructions, actually thrashing out who is going to cover what. What are you going to cover Mr. Krajisnik? Well, I don't know because we'll have to thrash this out in advance before we properly even know. What am I going to do, go down and see him at 3.00 in the morning to decide what we're actually going to ask the next day? It is really quite fantastic, the suggestion, Your Honour. The more I'm on my feet submitting the more the fantastic elements of it appear to emerge. It is simply not a helpful way for anybody to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers to withdraw just for a couple of minutes to see whether we can give a decision immediately so that everything's clear for the parties and for Mr. Krajisnik. We will adjourn. Please, would you remain standby. --- Break taken at 1.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber has considered your request and will give a decision on it and also give some reasons which may have a more -- which may be of a bit more general character. One of the consequences of the choice to be assisted by counsel and not to defend oneself is that counsel conducts the Defence, presents the Defence case at trial. Controlling the case presentation is a highly important aspect is of the professional responsibilities of Defence counsel. Counsel, I would say it goes almost without saying, will act in accordance with the instructions given to him by the accused. Any other division of labour, and I'm now talking about the work to be done in court, entails serious risks. I mention only two: Confusion among the Judges as to what exactly the Defence case is if inconsistencies in the case presentation would arise. The second, that the defendant may face the detrimental effect of any activity of himself that would disturb the tactical and strategic lines counsel have set out, and I do not even mention the lack of experience of most accused in trial techniques, including such matters as where to continue and where to stop questions on the subject at stake. These observations are sufficient to strictly stick to the system that counsel examines the witnesses, receiving information and instructions from the accused to that end. However, it is conceivable that exceptional circumstances might come into being. We will then, upon a submission by the accused showing good cause to deviate from the rule I just set out, decide. In respect of the present witness, no good cause has been shown. That's our decision in respect of your request. Then I think we should continue in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of September, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
